# Units of Augmentation One in Integral Group Rings

This study concerns the units of augmentation one in the integral group ring $\mathbb{Z}G$ of a finite group $G$. These units form a group that has long been a central object of investigation in the theory of integral group rings, as their structure reflects, in intricate ways, the structure of the underlying group $G$ itself.

The principal result of this work addresses the existence of certain elementary abelian subgroups among these units. Specifically, it is shown that a noncyclic subgroup of order $p^2$, for some odd prime $p$, can exist among the units of augmentation one only if such a subgroup already exists in $G$. In other words, the presence of a noncyclic group of order $p^2$ within the unit group forces the corresponding subgroup to be present in $G$ as well.

This result is significant because it establishes a correspondence between the subgroup structure of the units and that of the original group $G$. It thereby contributes to the broader program of understanding to what extent the arithmetic of $\mathbb{Z}G$ determines, and is determined by, the group-theoretic properties of $G$.

The case of the prime $p=2$ deserves separate attention. Here, the analogous statement holds as a consequence of the Brauer–Suzuki theorem, a deep result in the theory of finite groups concerning groups with quaternion Sylow $2$-subgroups. This connection to classical finite group theory underscores the depth of the correspondence being described.

Finally, it should be noted that this case for $p=2$ was recently observed by W. Kimmerle, whose work motivated and complements the results presented here for odd primes.

# Noncyclic Subgroups of Order $p^2$ in the Normalized Unit Group of $\mathbb{Z}G$

## Introduction

The study of the unit group of an integral group ring $\mathbb{Z}G$ of a finite group $G$ occupies a central place in modern representation theory and infinite group theory. A recurring theme in this area is the extent to which the arithmetic and combinatorial structure of the units of $\mathbb{Z}G$ is dictated by the structure of the underlying group $G$ itself. This paper examines one such structural question: the existence of noncyclic subgroups of order $p^2$ inside the group $V(\mathbb{Z}G)$ of units of augmentation one—the so-called *normalized units*.

The augmentation map $\varepsilon\colon \mathbb{Z}G \to \mathbb{Z}$, defined by sending each group element to $1$, gives rise to a natural splitting of the full unit group, and the normalized units $V(\mathbb{Z}G) = \ker(\varepsilon) \cap U(\mathbb{Z}G)$ form a subgroup containing $G$ as a natural embedded copy. Understanding how far the finite subgroups of $V(\mathbb{Z}G)$ deviate from those of $G$ lies at the heart of many classical conjectures, including the first Zassenhaus conjecture and the (now disproved in general, yet still influential) prime graph and Kimmerle conjectures.

## The Central Problem

In this work we focus on the finite $p$-subgroups of $V(\mathbb{Z}G)$, and specifically on the elementary question of whether $V(\mathbb{Z}G)$ can contain a *noncyclic* subgroup of order $p^2$—that is, a subgroup isomorphic to $C_p \times C_p$—when $G$ itself does not. Such subgroups are the smallest genuinely non-cyclic $p$-groups, and controlling their occurrence provides a fine-grained constraint on the local structure of the unit group.

Using purely group-theoretic methods, rather than the character-theoretic or module-theoretic machinery often deployed in this setting, we establish that for odd primes the answer is entirely governed by $G$.

## Main Result

Our principal theorem may be stated informally as follows: for an odd prime $p$, the normalized unit group $V(\mathbb{Z}G)$ contains a noncyclic subgroup of order $p^2$ **if and only if** $G$ already contains such a subgroup. In other words, the passage from $G$ to $V(\mathbb{Z}G)$ creates no new elementary abelian $p$-subgroups of rank two beyond those already present in the group. This confirms, in the case of order $p^2$, the expectation that the $p$-local structure of the unit group faithfully mirrors that of the finite group when $p$ is odd.

## The Case $p = 2$ and the Role of Brauer–Suzuki

The situation for the prime $2$ requires separate treatment and appeals to deeper structural results in finite group theory. Here the argument is completed by invoking the Brauer–Suzuki theorem, which controls groups possessing a generalized quaternion Sylow $2$-subgroup and, more broadly, restricts the way involutions and $2$-elements can interact within $G$. This complementary analysis ensures that the phenomenon described above extends across all primes, so that the complete picture—covering both the odd case treated by elementary group-theoretic techniques and the even case handled via Brauer–Suzuki—yields a uniform conclusion about the noncyclic $p^2$-subgroups of $V(\mathbb{Z}G)$.

## Consequences and Significance

Taken together, these results place strong constraints on the subgroup lattice of the normalized unit group. They demonstrate that the smallest noncyclic $p$-subgroups cannot appear "spuriously" as an artifact of the ring-theoretic enlargement of $G$, and they provide supporting evidence for the broader philosophy underlying the metabelian and prime graph questions: namely, that finite $p$-subgroups of $V(\mathbb{Z}G)$ are tightly bound to their counterparts inside $G$. The methods employed here, being group-theoretic in nature, are also of independent interest, offering a transparent route to conclusions that might otherwise be obtained only through more elaborate representation-theoretic considerations.

# The Brauer–Suzuki Theorem

The Brauer–Suzuki theorem is a fundamental result in the theory of finite groups, named after the mathematicians Richard Brauer and Michio Suzuki. It occupies an important place in the broader effort to understand and eventually classify the finite simple groups.

## Statement of the Theorem

In its most common formulation, the Brauer–Suzuki theorem addresses finite groups whose Sylow 2-subgroups are **generalized quaternion groups**. The theorem asserts that if a finite group $G$ has a generalized quaternion Sylow 2-subgroup, then $G$ cannot be simple. More precisely, such a group $G$ has a nontrivial center in the quotient $G/O(G)$, where $O(G)$ denotes the largest normal subgroup of odd order.

A key consequence is that the center of the factor group modulo the core of odd order contains an involution, which prevents the group from being a nonabelian simple group.

## Historical Context

The theorem was established in the early 1960s, during a period of intense activity in finite group theory. Richard Brauer, a pioneer of modular representation theory, and Michio Suzuki, known for his deep contributions to the study of simple groups, combined techniques from character theory to prove this result.

Their work relied heavily on **modular representation theory** and the analysis of characters, particularly the method of exceptional characters and block theory that Brauer had developed. This approach demonstrated the power of representation-theoretic tools in resolving purely group-theoretic questions.

## Significance

The Brauer–Suzuki theorem was a crucial early step toward the classification of finite simple groups, one of the greatest achievements of twentieth-century mathematics. By ruling out generalized quaternion groups as Sylow 2-subgroups of simple groups, it eliminated an entire class of potential configurations that researchers would otherwise have needed to consider.

The theorem exemplifies a recurring theme in the classification program: understanding the structure of a group by examining the properties of its Sylow subgroups. It stands alongside related results, such as the Feit–Thompson theorem, as a demonstration of how local structural constraints impose powerful global restrictions on finite groups.

## Legacy

Today, the Brauer–Suzuki theorem remains a standard reference in graduate courses and research on finite groups. It illustrates the fruitful interplay between abstract group theory and representation theory, and it continues to inspire methods used in modern algebraic research.

**Abstract**

Let $G$ be a finite group, $\mathbb{Z}G$ its integral group ring, and $V(\mathbb{Z}G)$ the group of units of augmentation one. Motivated by the Zassenhaus conjectures and, more specifically, by the question of which finite groups embed in $V(\mathbb{Z}G)$, we investigate the noncyclic subgroups of order $p^2$—that is, copies of the elementary abelian group $C_p \times C_p$—contained in $V(\mathbb{Z}G)$ for a prime $p$. Our main result shows that if $V(\mathbb{Z}G)$ contains a subgroup isomorphic to $C_p \times C_p$, then $G$ itself contains such a subgroup; equivalently, the $p$-rank of every finite $p$-subgroup of $V(\mathbb{Z}G)$ is bounded by the $p$-rank of $G$. This provides a strong analogue, in rank rather than order, of the classical results guaranteeing that elements of prime order in $V(\mathbb{Z}G)$ are conjugate in the rational group algebra to elements of $G$. The proof combines the theory of partial augmentations and the Luthar–Passi method with a careful analysis of the $p$-adic representations of the relevant sections of $G$, together with reductions to Frobenius and $p$-constrained situations. As applications, we verify the corresponding property of the prime graph and of the $\pi$-subgroup structure for several classes of groups, including groups with a normal Sylow $p$-subgroup and certain almost simple groups, and we exhibit examples showing that the rank bound is sharp and cannot in general be replaced by a statement about rational conjugacy of the whole subgroup.

**Abstract**

Let $G$ be a finite group, $\mathbb{Z}G$ its integral group ring, and $V(\mathbb{Z}G)$ the group of normalized units (units of augmentation $1$). A long-standing theme in the study of $V(\mathbb{Z}G)$, originating in the Zassenhaus conjectures and their weakenings, is the extent to which the finite-subgroup structure of $V(\mathbb{Z}G)$ is dictated by that of $G$. In this paper we prove the following: for every prime $p$, if $V(\mathbb{Z}G)$ contains a noncyclic subgroup of order $p^2$—equivalently, a subgroup isomorphic to $C_p \times C_p$—then $G$ itself contains such a subgroup. Consequently, whenever the Sylow $p$-subgroups of $G$ are cyclic, every $p$-subgroup of $V(\mathbb{Z}G)$ of order $p^2$ is cyclic, and more generally $V(\mathbb{Z}G)$ and $G$ have the same $p$-rank at the level $p^2$.

Our approach combines the theory of partial augmentations with a refinement of the HeLP (Hertweck–Luthar–Passi) method, using ordinary and modular character values to constrain the partial augmentations of the elements of a hypothetical $C_p \times C_p$. Hertweck's results on the $p$-adic conjugacy of $p$-elements, together with a fixed-point analysis of the associated $p$-modular representations, allow us to rule out the existence of a noncyclic order-$p^2$ subgroup absent from $G$. The argument is uniform in $p$ and does not require restrictions on $|G|$.

The theorem confirms, at the smallest noncyclic scale, the conjecture that the exponent-$p$ subgroup structure of $V(\mathbb{Z}G)$ embeds in that of $G$, and it supplies new evidence for the prime-graph and Kimmerle-type questions. We close by discussing obstructions to extending the method to arbitrary elementary abelian $p$-groups and to metacyclic $p$-subgroups.

*Keywords:* integral group ring, unit group, torsion units, partial augmentations, HeLP method, Zassenhaus conjecture.
